title: Gradient Descent II - Batch, Stochastic, Mini-Batch
abstract:
The three variants of gradient descent, distinguished by one decision: how much
data you look at before each parameter update. Batch uses the entire dataset and
makes one update per pass; stochastic uses one row at a time; mini-batch uses
small chunks and is what almost everything uses in practice. This document covers
each, the mathematics of why the gradient estimate is unbiased and why its noise
falls as $1/\sqrt{B}$, the epoch-versus-iteration vocabulary, why SGD's noise can
be an advantage, and the learning-rate schedules that make it converge.

blocks.t: Why the Noisy Gradient Still Works
The estimate is unbiased

The true gradient over the full dataset is
$\nabla L=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\nabla \ell_i$. Draw a batch $\mathcal{B}$ of size
$B$ uniformly at random and compute
\widehat{\nabla L}=\frac1B\sum_{i\in\mathcal B}\nabla \ell_i .
Then

\mathbb{E} \left[\widehat{
abla L}ight]
 = rac1B\sum_{i\in\mathcal B}\mathbb{E}\left[
abla \ell_iight]
 = rac1B\cdot B\cdot rac1n\sum_{j=1}^{n}

The mini-batch gradient is an unbiased estimate of the full gradient.
On average it points the right way — which is why taking many cheap, noisy steps
beats taking one expensive, exact step.
The noise falls as $1/\sqrt{B}$
For i.i.d. samples,

This single formula explains the standard batch sizes. Going from $B=1$ to
$B=32$ cuts the noise by a factor of $\sqrt{32}\approx5.7$ at 32 times the cost
per step — an excellent trade. Going from $B=32$ to $B=1024$ cuts it by a
further $5.7$ at 32 times the cost again — a poor trade. The returns
diminish as $\sqrt{B}$ while the cost grows as $B$, and the crossover is what
puts practical batch sizes in the 32–512 range.

blocks.t: Batch Gradient Descent

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Exact gradient — a smooth, deterministic path
Very slow: one update per full pass
Guaranteed convergence for a convex loss
Needs a lot of memory — the whole dataset at once
Cannot escape a local minimum in a non-convex loss
Impossible for datasets larger than RAM

blocks.t: Stochastic Gradient Descent

Updates after every single record. With 300 rows that is 300 updates per epoch,
against batch GD's one.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Works fast; used for big data
$O(p)$ memory — one row at a time
Never settles exactly at the minimum
No vectorisation — one row per operation is slow on modern hardware
The noise can escape shallow local minima
Needs a decaying learning rate to converge

blocks.cap:
On a non-convex loss, batch gradient descent is deterministic and
 settles into whichever basin it started in. SGD's gradient noise acts as a
 random perturbation that can carry it out of a shallow minimum — one reason
 the noise is not purely a defect.

blocks.t: Why SGD needs a decaying learning rate

With constant $\eta$, SGD does not converge to a point — it enters a
noise ball around the minimum of radius roughly proportional to
$\eta\sigma_g$, and bounces around inside it forever. To converge you must shrink
$\eta$. The classical Robbins–Monro conditions are

\sum_t \eta_t = \infty
 \quad\text{(you can still travel any distance)},
 \qquad
 \sum_t \eta_t^{2} < \infty
 \quad\text{(the noise dies out)} .

$\eta_t = \eta_0/t$ satisfies both; $\eta_t = \eta_0/\sqrt{t}$ satisfies the
first but not the second and is nonetheless common in practice.
Mini-Batch Gradient Descent
Why it is the default
It sits at the optimum of three separate curves at once:

items:
Noise falls as $1/\sqrt B$ — most of the benefit is captured
 by $B\approx32$.

Hardware. A GPU is a parallel machine; $B=1$ leaves it almost
 entirely idle, while $B=32$ or $256$ saturates it. A mini-batch step often
 costs barely more wall-clock time than a single-row step.

Memory is $O(Bp)$, so it is bounded by choice rather than by the
 dataset.

blocks.t: This is why the notes call it most widely used.
Powers of two, and shuffling

Batch sizes are conventionally powers of two (32, 64, 128, 256) because memory
alignment and GPU warp sizes make them marginally faster. More important:
shuffle the data every epoch. If the rows are ordered by class or by
time, un-shuffled mini-batches are not random samples, the gradient estimate is
biased, and training can oscillate badly.
The batch size interacts with the learning rate

Larger batches give less noisy gradients, which permits — and generally
requires — a larger learning rate. The common heuristic is the linear
scaling rule: if you multiply the batch size by $k$, multiply the learning rate
by $k$ as well. Increasing the batch size alone often makes training worse,
because the effective step size has fallen.
Code

import numpy as np, time
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, SGDRegressor
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 3000
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 5))
true_w = np.array([2.0, -1.0, 0.5, 3.0, -2.0])
y = X @ true_w + 7 + rng.normal(0, 1.0, n)

Xb = np.c_[np.ones(n), X]                    # intercept column
def full_loss(w):  return np.mean((y - Xb @ w) ** 2)

# =====================================================================
# 1. ALL THREE VARIANTS -- ONE function, batch_size is the only difference
# =====================================================================
def gradient_descent(Xb, y, batch_size, lr=0.05, epochs=30, seed=0):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n, p = Xb.shape
    w = np.zeros(p)
    updates, history = 0, []

    for epoch in range(epochs):
        idx = r.permutation(n)               # SHUFFLE every epoch
        for start in range(0, n, batch_size):
            b  = idx[start:start + batch_size]
            Xb_, y_ = Xb[b], y[b]
            # the mini-batch gradient -- identical formula, fewer rows
            grad = -(2 / len(b)) * Xb_.T @ (y_ - Xb_ @ w)
            w -= lr * grad
            updates += 1
        history.append(np.mean((y - Xb @ w) ** 2))
    return w, updates, history

variants = {
    "Batch GD      (B=n)":  n,     # ONE update per epoch
    "Stochastic GD (B=1)":  1,     # n updates per epoch
    "Mini-batch    (B=32)": 32,    # n/32 updates per epoch
}

print(f"{'variant':22s} {'updates/epoch':>14s} {'final loss':>12s} {'time':>9s}")
for name, B in variants.items():
    lr = 0.05 if B > 1 else 0.005            # SGD needs a smaller rate
    t = time.perf_counter()
    w, upd, hist = gradient_descent(Xb, y, B, lr=lr, epochs=30)
    el = time.perf_counter() - t
    print(f"{name:22s} {upd//30:14d} {hist[-1]:12.5f} {el:8.3f}s")

print(f"\ntrue weights : {np.r_[7.0, true_w]}")
print(f"OLS          : {np.r_[LinearRegression().fit(X,y).intercept_, LinearRegression().fit(X,y).coef_].round(3)}")

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE GRADIENT ESTIMATE IS UNBIASED
# =====================================================================
w0 = np.zeros(6)
true_grad = -(2/n) * Xb.T @ (y - Xb @ w0)

for B in [1, 8, 32, 128]:
    ests = []
    for _ in range(4000):
        b = rng.choice(n, B, replace=False)
        ests.append(-(2/B) * Xb[b].T @ (y[b] - Xb[b] @ w0))
    ests = np.array(ests)
    bias = np.abs(ests.mean(axis=0) - true_grad).max()
    print(f"B={B:4d}  max bias {bias:.5f}   mean noise sd {ests.std(axis=0).mean():.4f}")
# Bias ~ 0 for every B: the estimate is UNBIASED regardless of batch size.

# =====================================================================
# 3. THE NOISE FALLS AS 1/sqrt(B)
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'B':>6s} {'grad sd':>10s} {'sd * sqrt(B)':>14s}")
for B in [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512]:
    ests = np.array([-(2/B) * Xb[b].T @ (y[b] - Xb[b] @ w0)
                     for b in (rng.choice(n, B, replace=False) for _ in range(600))])
    sd = ests.std(axis=0).mean()
    print(f"{B:6d} {sd:10.4f} {sd*np.sqrt(B):14.4f}")
# The last column is CONSTANT -- confirming sd proportional to 1/sqrt(B).
# Doubling B from 32 to 64 buys only a 1.41x noise reduction for 2x the cost.

# =====================================================================
# 4. PROGRESS PER EPOCH vs PROGRESS PER UPDATE
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'variant':22s} {'loss @ epoch 1':>16s} {'loss @ epoch 30':>17s}")
for name, B in variants.items():
    lr = 0.05 if B > 1 else 0.005
    _, _, h = gradient_descent(Xb, y, B, lr=lr, epochs=30)
    print(f"{name:22s} {h[0]:16.4f} {h[-1]:17.5f}")
# After ONE epoch, SGD and mini-batch have already nearly converged;
# batch GD has taken a single step.

# =====================================================================
# 5. SGD DOES NOT SETTLE -- it orbits in a noise ball
# =====================================================================
def sgd_trace(lr, decay=False, epochs=60):
    r = np.random.default_rng(1); w = np.zeros(6); hist = []
    for ep in range(epochs):
        eta = lr / (1 + ep) if decay else lr          # Robbins-Monro 1/t
        for i in r.permutation(n):
            g = -2 * Xb[i] * (y[i] - Xb[i] @ w)
            w -= eta * g
        hist.append(full_loss(w))
    return hist

const = sgd_trace(0.004, decay=False)
decay = sgd_trace(0.004, decay=True)
print(f"\nconstant lr: loss over the last 10 epochs varies by "
      f"{np.ptp(const[-10:]):.5f}")
print(f"decaying lr: loss over the last 10 epochs varies by "
      f"{np.ptp(decay[-10:]):.5f}   <- it settles")

# =====================================================================
# 6. THE LINEAR SCALING RULE -- batch size and learning rate interact
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'B':>6s} {'lr fixed 0.01':>16s} {'lr scaled':>12s}")
for B in [8, 32, 128, 512]:
    _, _, h_fixed  = gradient_descent(Xb, y, B, lr=0.01,              epochs=20)
    _, _, h_scaled = gradient_descent(Xb, y, B, lr=0.01 * (B / 8),    epochs=20)
    print(f"{B:6d} {h_fixed[-1]:16.5f} {h_scaled[-1]:12.5f}")
# With lr fixed, larger batches get WORSE -- fewer updates at the same step size.
# Scaling lr with B keeps the effective progress per epoch roughly constant.

# =====================================================================
# 7. SHUFFLING IS NOT OPTIONAL
# =====================================================================
order = np.argsort(y)                       # data sorted by the target
Xs, ys = Xb[order], y[order]

def no_shuffle(Xb, y, B=32, lr=0.05, epochs=30):
    w = np.zeros(Xb.shape[1])
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for s in range(0, len(y), B):        # sequential, never shuffled
            b = slice(s, s + B)
            w -= lr * (-(2/len(y[b])) * Xb[b].T @ (y[b] - Xb[b] @ w))
    return np.mean((y - Xb @ w) ** 2)

print(f"\nshuffled     final loss {gradient_descent(Xs, ys, 32)[2][-1]:.5f}")
print(f"NOT shuffled final loss {no_shuffle(Xs, ys):.5f}")
# Un-shuffled batches are not random samples, so the gradient is biased
# within each pass and training oscillates.

# =====================================================================
# 8. SKLEARN
# =====================================================================
# SGDRegressor is TRUE stochastic GD (one sample at a time):
sgd = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    SGDRegressor(learning_rate="invscaling", eta0=0.01,
                                 max_iter=1000, tol=1e-5, random_state=0)).fit(X, y)
print("\nSGDRegressor coef:", sgd.named_steps["sgdregressor"].coef_.round(3))

# For MINI-batch, use partial_fit over chunks -- this is also how you do
# out-of-core and online learning (Topic 03):
mb = SGDRegressor(learning_rate="constant", eta0=0.01, random_state=0)
sc = StandardScaler().fit(X)
Xz = sc.transform(X)
for epoch in range(30):
    idx = rng.permutation(n)
    for s in range(0, n, 64):
        b = idx[s:s+64]
        mb.partial_fit(Xz[b], y[b])          # one mini-batch update
print("mini-batch via partial_fit:", mb.coef_.round(3))
print("true (scaled space)       :", (true_w * sc.scale_).round(3))
Worked Examples
One epoch with batch, stochastic and mini-batch updates
Data $x = [1,2,3,4]$, $y = [2,4,6,8]$ (true slope 2), learning rate $\eta = 0.05$, start $m=0$. One epoch means one pass over the four points.
Batch GD: one update from all four points. Gradient of the mean squared error at $m=0$:
m \leftarrow 0 - 0.05\cdot(-30) = 1.5
After one epoch, batch GD has made 1 update and sits at $m = 1.5$.
Stochastic GD: one update per point. Each step uses a single $(x_i,y_i)$ and the updated $m$ feeds the next point. Per-point gradient is $-2x_i(y_i - m x_i)$:
After one epoch SGD has made 4 updates and reached $m = 2.065$, already close to the answer. Each step is noisy (the second point alone pushes $m$ up to $0.92$), but each step is cheap.
Mini-batch GD (size 2). Batches $\{(1,2),(2,4)\}$ and $\{(3,6),(4,8)\}$ give 2 updates per epoch, and the result after the epoch is $m = 2.375$ (computed with the batch gradient for each pair).
Trade-off. Batch: one smooth step, expensive per step. Stochastic: many noisy steps, cheap each. Mini-batch: the usual compromise, and the one that vectorised hardware runs fastest.

The loop: for each batch — compute loss, compute gradient,
 update $m$ and $c$; repeat for each batch, then for each epoch.

An epoch is one pass over the data; an iteration is one
 parameter update. Batch: 1 update/epoch. SGD: $n$. Mini-batch: $n/B$.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Batch, stochastic or mini-batch — which and why?

Mini-batch, almost always. It captures most of the noise reduction (which falls
only as $1/\sqrt B$), it vectorises so hardware is used efficiently, and its
memory is bounded by choice rather than by the dataset. Pure batch is too slow and
memory-hungry; pure SGD wastes modern hardware and fluctuates heavily.
Q. If the mini-batch gradient is only an estimate, why does it work?

Because it is unbiased — its expectation is exactly the full gradient. On
average each step points the right way, and taking many cheap, slightly wrong
steps reaches the minimum faster than taking one expensive, exactly right step.
Q. Why is 32 such a common batch size?

Because gradient noise falls as $1/\sqrt B$ while cost grows as $B$. Going from
1 to 32 cuts the noise by $5.7\times$; going from 32 to 1024 cuts it by another
$5.7\times$ at 32 times the cost. The returns diminish exactly where the hardware
starts being well utilised.
Q. Why does SGD need a decaying learning rate?

With constant $\eta$ the gradient noise never vanishes, so the parameters bounce
around inside a noise ball of radius proportional to $\eta\sigma_g$ rather than
converging. Shrinking $\eta$ shrinks the ball. Robbins–Monro gives the formal
conditions.
Q. You increased the batch size and training got worse. Why?

Because you did not increase the learning rate. A larger batch means fewer updates
per epoch at the same step size, so less total progress. The linear scaling rule
says to multiply $\eta$ by the same factor you multiplied $B$ by.
Q. Is SGD's noise purely a disadvantage?

No. On a non-convex loss — every neural network — the noise acts as a random
perturbation that can carry the parameters out of a sharp or shallow local
minimum, and it is widely believed to bias training towards flatter minima, which
generalise better. It is also a mild form of regularisation.
Q. Why must you shuffle each epoch?

Because a mini-batch must be a random sample for the gradient estimate to be
unbiased. If the data is ordered by class or by time, sequential batches are
systematically biased, and the parameters oscillate as each pass sweeps through the
ordering.
